blurb: Why robots lag behind chatbots, the new robot "brains", how self-driving cars see the road, and the push for humanoids.

steps.p: Computers beat grandmasters at chess decades ago, yet folding a towel is still tough. That's Moravec's paradox.
Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years perfecting our movement and senses, so they feel effortless. Abstract reasoning is new to us, so it feels hard.
steps.analogy: We don't notice how hard walking is because our bodies do it for us.

steps.p: Chatbots learned from trillions of words online. There's no equivalent pile of recorded robot movements to learn from.
So people remotely control robots to demonstrate tasks (teleoperation), recording every movement — slow and expensive.
A wrong word can be deleted; a dropped glass breaks. And every kitchen, light and object is a little different.

options: Reasoning is relatively easy for machines, while basic perception and movement are hard
Chess is harder than folding towels for humans
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 1.
cards.why: Easy and hard are flipped. What feels effortless to us took evolution ages to build, and is hardest to copy.

cards.statement: Robotics has an internet-sized dataset of robot actions, like the text that trains chatbots.
cards.why: False. Robot data has to be collected physically and is tiny by comparison. That's a central bottleneck.

cards.q: A common way to collect robot training data is…
options: Teleoperation: people remotely control robots to demonstrate tasks
cards.why: Teleoperation. A person "drives" the robot through a task; the recorded movements become examples to learn from.

cards.title: In 2023, 21 institutions pooled their robot data into one dataset spanning 22 robot types.
cards.detail: The Open X-Embodiment project, led by Google DeepMind, gathered over a million robot episodes. Models trained on the mix often beat ones trained on a single robot.

cards.statement: A robot trained in one kitchen often struggles when moved to a different kitchen.
cards.why: True. New lighting, layouts and objects can confuse it. Handling new places is a major goal of robot research.

steps.p: Take a model that already understands images and words from the internet.
Train it on robot data so, instead of words, it outputs actions: move the arm here, close the gripper. That's a vision-language-action model.
Because it learned from the web, it can follow instructions about things it never handled — "pick up the extinct animal" → the toy dinosaur.
Predicting short bursts of future movements at once (action chunking) gives smoother, more confident motion than one tiny step at a time.
steps.analogy: Planning a whole dance step rather than deciding each muscle twitch separately.

steps.p: Rigid blocks are easy to model. Cloth, food and cables take endless shapes, which makes tasks like folding laundry a real test.

options: Robot actions, such as arm movements and gripper commands
cards.why: Actions. It sees, reads the instruction, and directly produces movements.

cards.statement: Google's RT-2 could follow instructions involving things missing from its robot training data, thanks to web pretraining.
cards.why: True. Knowledge from internet images and text carried over into physical actions.

options: Predicts a short sequence of future movements at once, giving smoother motion
cards.why: Planning a burst. It reduces jitter and hesitation compared with deciding each tiny motion separately.

cards.title: Physical Intelligence's π0 model folded laundry taken straight from a basket.
cards.detail: Laundry is notoriously hard for robots because cloth has endless shapes. The 2024 demo was seen as a milestone for general-purpose robot hands.

cards.q: Why are soft things like clothes especially hard for robots?
options: They can take endless shapes and are hard to predict or simulate
cards.why: Endless shapes. A shirt can be crumpled a million ways, and each needs a different grasp.

steps.p: Cameras, radar and lidar build a 3D picture of everything around: cars, cyclists, cones, lane lines.
Lidar fires laser pulses and times how long they take to bounce back, measuring distances very precisely all around the car.
steps.analogy: Like a bat's echolocation, but with light.

steps.p: It forecasts what everyone else will do next — will that pedestrian step out? Will that car change lanes?
It chooses a safe, smooth path and speed, many times per second.
Level 2 helps but needs your constant attention. Level 4 drives with nobody at the wheel, within a set area and conditions.

options: Timing how long laser pulses take to bounce back
cards.why: Timing laser echoes. Light's speed is known, so the delay gives the exact distance.

options: Can drive with no human driver within a set area and conditions
Needs a driver's hands on the wheel
Can drive anywhere on Earth in any weather
cards.why: Driverless, within limits. Waymo's robotaxis are Level 4: no one in the driver's seat, but only in mapped service areas.

cards.title: In the 2004 DARPA Grand Challenge, no self-driving car finished — the best managed about 7 miles of a 150-mile course.
cards.detail: A year later five vehicles finished, led by Stanford's Stanley. Many of the engineers went on to found the self-driving industry.

cards.statement: Tesla's standard Autopilot is a Level 4 system that needs no driver attention.
cards.why: False. It's a Level 2 driver-assistance system: the driver must stay attentive and ready to take over.

cards.statement: Waymo runs fully driverless, paid robotaxi rides in several US cities.
cards.why: True. Including Phoenix, San Francisco and Los Angeles, with no safety driver on board.

cards.title: Why build robots shaped like us?

steps.p: Stairs, door handles, shelves and tools are all designed for human bodies. A human-shaped robot could use them without rebuilding everything.
A humanoid can learn by copying videos and demonstrations of people more directly than a robot with wheels and one arm.
Our hands have about 27 bones, fine control and rich touch sensing. Matching that is extremely difficult.
steps.analogy: Try buttoning a shirt in thick ski gloves — that's many robot hands today.

steps.p: Prices have fallen fast. China's Unitree priced its G1 humanoid from about $16,000 in 2024.
Polished videos may be remote-controlled, sped up or the best of many tries. Reliable, all-day useful work is still rare.

cards.q: The main argument for making general-purpose robots human-shaped is…
options: Our homes, workplaces and tools are designed for human bodies
It's cheaper than any other shape
cards.why: Fit the world as it is. Rather than redesigning buildings for robots, build robots that fit buildings.

cards.statement: Boston Dynamics retired its hydraulic Atlas robot and unveiled an all-electric version in 2024.
cards.why: True. The electric Atlas is aimed at practical work, starting in car factories with Hyundai.

cards.q: What's often called the hardest part of a humanoid to get right?
options: Dexterous hands with fine control and touch
cards.hint: Buttoning a shirt in ski gloves.
cards.why: The hands. Grasping varied objects gently and precisely needs many joints and sensitive touch.

cards.title: Chinese maker Unitree priced its G1 humanoid from about $16,000 in 2024.
cards.detail: That was a fraction of earlier humanoids' cost, reflecting China's strength in robot hardware and parts.

cards.title: Watch robot demos like a sceptic
cards.body: Check for words like "teleoperated" or "autonomous", whether the video is sped up, and how many takes it needed.
cards.challenge: Find a recent humanoid robot video and look for whether it was autonomous or remote-controlled.
